subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If Q(h,k) is the image of the point P(x₁,y₁) with respect to the straight line ax+by+c=0 then prove that (h−x₁) : a = (k−y₁) : b = −2(ax₁+by₁+c) : (a²+b²).

mark_split.label: Write h and k through r

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.18 — LAQ chapter 1 The Straight Line, answer 5.2. Printed appearance: AP 19. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this LAQ chapter. It is not a bare guess: the book prints its own numbered 'Step-1 / Step-2 / Step-3' structure against this very answer, and the split follows those printed steps, giving the two long eliminations two marks each and the closing solve two, with one for setting up. The only printed splits in this UNIT are on SAQ answer 59 (book p.63, 1+1+2) and VSAQ answer 98 (p.83, 1+1) — both shorter cuts, so neither fixes a 7-mark shape. Paper position: Maths-1B Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. ⚠ The book prints a note between answers 5.1 and 5.2 reading 'First half of the solution is same to same' — the two proofs share their first three steps EXACTLY, and differ only in the closing condition. The step ids and labels here are deliberately identical across the two files for that reason, which follows the Maths-1A precedent of giving one method over different conditions one shared skeleton. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. NOTE: The Straight Line is the FIRST Maths-1B unit to occupy ALL THREE sections of the paper — the book's IPE Blue Print (book p.3) gives it 2+2 marks in Section A, 4 in Section B and 7 in Section C, 15 in all, tying Differentiation as the highest-scoring unit on the paper. It therefore has three separate chapters in this book: LAQ chapter 1 (book pp.14-18), SAQ chapter 9 (pp.61-64) and VSAQ chapter 14 (pp.79-82). All three boundaries were walked: p.19 opens Pair of Straight Lines, p.65 opens Limits & Continuity, and p.83 opens 3-D Coordinates. The book's separate STAR QUESTIONS PLUS bank (pp.104-108) contributes three more, answers 182-184, authored here as sqp1-sqp3. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Find r from the condition.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say what perpendicularity gives you, and what condition on Q finishes it.

steps.label: Both slopes
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two slopes are needed — the one joining the two points, and the one of the given line. The second reads straight off the coefficients as −a/b.
steps.memory_tip: The slope of PQ and the line's own slope −a/b.
lines: Slope of PQ is  m₁ = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = (k − y₁)/(h − x₁)
Slope of the line ax + by + c = 0 is  m₂ = −a/b

recall.must_convey: That the slope of PQ is (k − y₁)/(h − x₁) and the slope of the line is −a/b.
accept: slope of P Q is k minus y one over h minus x one and the line's slope is minus a over b
write both slopes, one from the two points and one from the coefficients
the line a x plus b y plus c has slope minus a over b
rendu slopes rayali, P Q di and line di
both slopes first

steps.why: Everything in this proof follows from PQ being perpendicular to the line, so both slopes have to be on the page before that fact can be used.
common_mistakes: Writing the slope of PQ upside down.

steps.label: Draw P, the line and the image
steps.margin_note: Worth no mark but worth drawing, and it is the picture that explains the factor 2. Q is the mirror point, so the line cuts PQ in HALF — the two tick marks are equal, and it is the MIDPOINT R that lies on the line, not Q.
steps.memory_tip: The picture explains the factor 2: the line cuts PQ in HALF, so it is the MIDPOINT that lies on it.

recall.must_convey: That P, the line, the image Q and the midpoint R on the line are sketched, with PR = RQ. Naming the drawing is full credit — it cannot be spoken.
accept: draw P above the line and its mirror image Q below with the midpoint on the line
sketch the point, the line, and the image with equal halves
show R the midpoint of P Q lying on the line
P ki image Q ni line kinda geesi midpoint mark cheyyali
draw the image of the point in the line

steps.why: An image is the mirror point, so the line is the perpendicular BISECTOR of PQ. Q itself is NOT on the line — its midpoint with P is, and halving inside the equation is what doubles the answer.
common_mistakes: Drawing Q on the line, which makes it the foot of the perpendicular instead.
Drawing PR and RQ unequal, which loses the bisection the proof depends on.

steps.label: Use the perpendicularity
steps.margin_note: Two marks. PQ meets the line at a right angle, so m₁m₂ = −1. Rearranged, that says (h − x₁)/a and (k − y₁)/b are EQUAL — and giving that common value the name r is what makes the rest of the proof short.
steps.memory_tip: m₁m₂ = −1 makes the two ratios equal; call the common value r.

recall.must_convey: That m₁m₂ = −1 gives (h − x₁)/a = (k − y₁)/b, and this common value is named r.
accept: perpendicular means m one m two equals minus one, rearrange and call the common value r
the product of the slopes is minus one
h minus x one over a equals k minus y one over b, take it as r
perpendicular kabatti m one into m two equals minus one
name the common ratio r

steps.why: Naming the common ratio r converts two unknowns h and k into ONE unknown, which is the move that makes a two-variable problem solvable in a line.
common_mistakes: Keeping h and k separate and ending with two unknowns and one equation.

steps.label: Write h and k through r
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Read (1) both ways round: each of h and k is now its P-coordinate plus a multiple of r. The point Q is pinned by the single number r.
steps.memory_tip: h and k are each P's coordinate plus a multiple of r.
lines: ∴ (h − x₁)/a = r  ⇒  h − x₁ = ar  ⇒  h = x₁ + ar
(k − y₁)/b = r  ⇒  k − y₁ = br  ⇒  k = y₁ + br

recall.must_convey: That h = x₁ + ar and k = y₁ + br.
accept: h is x one plus a r and k is y one plus b r
read the ratio both ways to get h and k in terms of r
express both coordinates through r
h equals x one plus a r, k equals y one plus b r
write h and k using r
heard_as: h equals x one plus a r
k equals y one plus b r

steps.why: With h and k both written through r, any single condition on Q becomes a single equation in r — and that condition is the only place the two proofs differ.
common_mistakes: Writing h = x₁ + br and k = y₁ + ar, with a and b swapped.
Dropping the x₁ or y₁ when rearranging.

steps.label: Find r from the condition
steps.margin_note: The last three marks, and the ONLY place this proof differs from its neighbour. The IMAGE is the mirror point, so the line bisects PQ — it is the MIDPOINT R that lies on the line, not Q itself. That midpoint is where the factor 2 in the answer comes from.
steps.memory_tip: The IMAGE is a mirror point, so the MIDPOINT lies on the line, not Q — and that is where the 2 comes from.
lines: Now P = (x₁, y₁), Q = (h, k) ⇒ Mid point of PQ is
But R lies on ax + by + c = 0

recall.must_convey: That the MIDPOINT of PQ lies on the line, giving r = −2(ax₁+by₁+c)/(a²+b²).

steps.why: An image is the mirror point, so the line is the perpendicular BISECTOR of PQ — Q itself is not on the line, its midpoint with P is. Halving inside the equation is what doubles the final numerator.
common_mistakes: Putting Q on the line, which gives the foot-of-perpendicular answer with no factor 2.
Forgetting to multiply the constant c by 2 when clearing the halves.
